units.text: A glass box at the end of nowhere.
A fan turns in one corner.
LEILANI KANE, 50, in a reflective vest, sits with a voice recorder pressed to her mouth and a thermos steaming at her elbow.
Day eleven. I said I'd do this every night. I'm doing it.
units.name: LEILANI

units.text: Nobody has come through since two-forty. A truck, then nothing. I counted the trucks on the first night, you know. Eighty-one. Last night, nine. They've found another road. That's what I would do. I'd find another road.
units.name: LEILANI

units.text: This is Leilani Kane. If you are hearing this, either I am dead or I got brave. Probably I am neither. Probably I am in the booth with a thermos telling the dark what it already knows.
units.name: LEILANI

units.text: That's from March. March, Leilani. You were so sure you'd be somewhere else.
units.name: LEILANI

units.text: I'm going to say a thing now. I haven't said it to anyone. When the state sold the road to the company, I thought, fine, fine, I'll stay on. They'll need somebody. And there was a letter, and the letter said my position had been eliminated, effective the first, and I read it, and I folded it, and I came to work. Seven weeks. Nobody noticed. Nobody has paid me since August.
units.name: LEILANI

units.text: She looks at the barrier arm, a red-and-white bar pointing at the sky.
I keep the arm up. Isn't that something? There's nothing to stop. There's no one to stop. I keep the arm up so they'll know the road is still open.
units.name: LEILANI

units.text: In the sudden quiet she holds the recorder in both hands.
If you're hearing this, I'm going home now. I'm going to leave the lights on. If a car comes through, it can have the road.
units.name: LEILANI

units.text: Leaves the recorder on the counter, red light glowing.
